name: Kokoda
summary: Raw fish cured in lime juice and finished in coconut milk with onion, tomato and chilli, often called Fijian ceviche.
story: Kokoda is Fiji's best-known raw-fish dish. Fresh fish, traditionally a firm white-fleshed species, is soaked in citrus juice until it turns opaque, then dressed with coconut milk and chopped vegetables. It is served cold, often in a coconut shell or a bowl, as a starter or light main. Similar raw-fish-in-citrus dishes exist across the Pacific, each with its own name.

origin_claims.claim: Raw fish cured in citrus is a widespread Pacific tradition; kokoda is the Fijian version.

name: Lovo
summary: A Fijian feast cooked in an earth oven of heated stones, with meat, fish, cassava and taro wrapped in leaves.
story: Lovo is Fiji's earth oven. A fire heats stones in a pit, food wrapped in banana or other leaves is laid on the stones, covered, and left to steam for several hours. It is used for village feasts, weddings, church events and celebrations, and gives the food a gentle smoky flavour. Similar earth ovens exist across the Pacific under different names, such as the Māori hāngī.

origin_claims.claim: Earth-oven cooking is a long-established Pacific tradition and the usual way to feed large gatherings in Fiji.

name: Rourou
summary: Young taro leaves slowly simmered in coconut milk, a soft green side dish served at everyday and festive meals.
story: Rourou is made from the leaves of the dalo (taro) plant, cooked until soft in coconut milk with onion. The leaves must be cooked thoroughly, which makes them mild and silky. It is a very common accompaniment to boiled root crops and fish, and appears at both everyday family meals and feasts.

origin_claims.claim: Taro leaves cooked in coconut milk are a long-standing staple across the Pacific.

name: Vakalolo
summary: A sweet pudding of grated cassava baked with coconut cream and sugar and served with a coconut syrup.
story: Vakalolo is a sweet pudding from Fijian and wider Pacific tradition, made from grated root crops such as cassava or taro, coconut cream and sugar, traditionally wrapped in leaves and cooked in the lovo. It is a feast and celebration dish. Versions differ from island to island and in different households.

origin_claims.claim: A traditional sweet pudding of root crop and coconut cooked at feasts.

name: Yaqona
summary: The Fijian name for kava, an earthy, numbing drink made by steeping ground kava root in water.
story: Yaqona is made from the root of the kava plant, pounded or ground and mixed with water in a large bowl called a tanoa. Served in cups made from coconut shell (bilo), it is central to Fijian ceremony: welcoming guests, sealing agreements, and marking weddings, funerals and chiefly events. The drink is mildly numbing to the lips and tongue, and has a distinct earthy taste.

origin_claims.claim: Kava drinking is a deeply rooted ceremonial tradition across Fiji and the wider Pacific.

name: Fijian dhal
summary: A thin, golden yellow split-pea soup tempered with fried garlic and cumin, eaten with rice or roti.
story: Dhal came to Fiji with Indian indentured labourers from the late 19th century and has become an everyday dish in Indo-Fijian homes and well beyond them. In Fiji it is usually a fairly thin soup of yellow split peas, turmeric and a garlic-and-cumin seasoning fried in oil and poured over at the end. It is eaten with rice or roti and often alongside a curry.

origin_claims.claim: Brought by Indian indentured labourers who arrived from 1879 and now an everyday Fiji dish.

name: Fijian goat curry
summary: Goat simmered with onion, garlic, ginger and curry powder until tender, a favourite Indo-Fijian family dish.
story: Curry is one of the signatures of Indo-Fijian cooking, made with the spices the community's ancestors brought from India and adapted over time to local ingredients. Goat is a popular meat for festive and weekend meals, cooked slowly on the bone with potato until the sauce thickens. It is eaten with rice or roti.

origin_claims.claim: Indo-Fijian curries derive from the South Asian traditions of indentured labourers who came from 1879.

name: Besan ladoo
summary: Round sweets of gram flour roasted in ghee and bound with sugar and cardamom, made for Diwali and other celebrations.
story: Besan ladoo are a sweet from the Indian subcontinent that came to Fiji with the Indo-Fijian community. Gram (chickpea) flour is slowly roasted in ghee until nutty, then sweetened and rolled into balls. They are made and exchanged at Diwali, weddings and religious occasions, and are common in sweet shops.

origin_claims.claim: Part of the sweet-making tradition brought by Indo-Fijians from India.

name: Fijian samosa
summary: Crisp fried pastry triangles filled with spiced potato and peas, sold in markets and snack shops.
story: Samosas came to Fiji with the Indo-Fijian community and are now a common snack at market stalls, bakeries, and sweet shops, usually eaten with chutney or tamarind sauce. Potato and pea is the standard vegetarian filling. They are also made at home for festivals such as Diwali.

origin_claims.claim: A South Asian snack brought to Fiji by Indian labourers and their descendants.

name: Duruka in coconut milk
summary: The tender flower shoots of the duruka cane plant, simmered in coconut milk with onion and chilli.
story: Duruka (Saccharum edule), often called Fiji asparagus, is a cane-like plant whose unopened flower heads are harvested as a seasonal vegetable. They are boiled or simmered in coconut milk and eaten as a side with rice and root crops or fish. The harvest season is short, so it is a seasonal treat.

origin_claims.claim: A seasonal vegetable eaten in Fiji and parts of Melanesia, traditionally cooked in coconut milk.
